evidence: This reports specific model performance for NSCLC at a particular time interval.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main finding.

claim: A model on how RNA biomarkers can be utilized in clinical settings was proposed.
source: We also proposed a model on how RNA biomarkers can be utilized in clinical settings.
evidence: This is a statement about a contribution of the study.

claim: Top performing models can produce AUCs up to 0.9 before diagnosis suggesting a great potential for LC early prediction.
source: Our top performing models can produce AUCs up to 0.9 before diagnosis suggesting a great potential for LC early prediction.
evidence: This is a summary of the best model performance and its implications.

claim: The study used the population-based Janus Serum Bank (JSB) cohort containing prediagnostic serum samples.
source: We used the population-based Janus Serum Bank (JSB) cohort containing prediagnostic serum samples (Langseth et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the source of the samples used in the study.

claim: The study participants were identified by linking the JSB to the CRN.
source: The study participants were identified by linking the JSB to the CRN.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying study participants.

claim: The analyses were restricted to patients later diagnosed with LC up to 10 years after blood donation and control samples from individuals cancer-free (except non-melanoma skin cancer) at least 10 years after sample collection.
source: We restricted our analyses to patients later diagnosed with LC up to 10 years after blood donation and control samples from individuals cancer-free (except non-melanoma skin cancer) at least 10 years after sample collection.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Cases and controls were matched on confounders.
source: We matched cases and controls on confounders (see Bioinformatics analyses).
evidence: This describes the matching strategy used in the study.

claim: Smoking, collected from health survey data, was classified as current, former, or never smokers.
source: Smoking, collected from health survey data, was classified as current, former, or never smokers (Hjerkind et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes how smoking status was determined.

claim: Smoking significantly affects RNA expression levels.
source: Since we have previously shown that smoking significantly affects RNA expression levels, we only included smokers (i.e. current and former) in the initial analyses and model building.
evidence: This is a statement based on previous findings, used to justify the study design.

claim: Detailed cancer information was selected from the CRN that has systematically collected mandatory notification on cancer occurrence for the Norwegian population since 1952.
source: Detailed cancer information was selected from the CRN that has systematically collected mandatory notification on cancer occurrence for the Norwegian population since 1952 (Larsen et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the source of cancer information.

claim: The cases were classified into histological subtypes: NSCLC, SCLC, and others, the latter referring to other less defined or multiple histologies.
source: The cases were classified into histological subtypes: NSCLC, SCLC, and others, the latter referring to other less defined or multiple histologies.
evidence: This describes the histological classification used in the study.

claim: Stage at diagnosis was encoded with the TNM system: early (localized – stage I), locally advanced (regional – stages II and III), advanced or metastatic (distant – stage IV), and unknown.
source: Stage at diagnosis was encoded with the TNM system: early (localized – stage I), locally advanced (regional – stages II and III), advanced or metastatic (distant – stage IV), and unknown (Cancer Registry of Norway, 2020).
evidence: This describes the staging system used in the study.

claim: RNA was extracted from 400 µL serum using phenol-chloroform and miRNeasy Serum/Plasma kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA).
source: We extracted RNA from 400 µL serum using phenol-chloroform and miRNeasy Serum/Plasma kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA).
evidence: This describes the RNA extraction method.

claim: Size selection was performed using a 3% Agarose Gel Cassette (Cat. No CSD3010) on a Pippin Prep (Sage Science) with a cut size optimized to cover RNA molecules from 17 to 47 nt in length.
source: We performed size selection using a 3% Agarose Gel Cassette (Cat. No CSD3010) on a Pippin Prep (Sage Science) with a cut size optimized to cover RNA molecules from 17 to 47 nt in length.
evidence: This describes the size selection method.

claim: Libraries were prepared with the NEBNext Small RNA kit (NEB, Ipswich, MA) and sequenced on a HiSeq 2500 platform to on average 18 million sequences per sample (Illumina, San Diego, CA).
source: Libraries were prepared with the NEBNext Small RNA kit (NEB, Ipswich, MA) and sequenced on a HiSeq 2500 platform to on average 18 million sequences per sample (Illumina, San Diego, CA).
evidence: This describes the library preparation and sequencing method.

claim: The bioinformatics workflow includes quality control, adapter trimming, read mapping, read counting, and creation of count tables.
source: Our bioinformatics workflow includes quality control, adapter trimming, read mapping, read counting, and creation of count tables.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics analysis pipeline.

claim: A large annotation dataset containing several RNA classes available in serum was used, including miRBase (v22.1) for miRNAs, piRBase (v1.0) for piRNAs, and the GENCODE (v26) for other RNA classes.
source: We used a large annotation dataset containing several RNA classes available in serum (Umu et al., 2018), including miRBase (v22.1) for miRNAs (Kozomara et al., 2019), piRBase (v1.0) for piRNAs (Zhang et al., 2014), and the GENCODE (v26) for other RNA classes (Harrow et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the annotation databases used for RNA identification.

claim: The AdapterRemoval tool was used for adapter trimming.
source: We used the AdapterRemoval tool for adapter trimming (Schubert et al., 2016) and Bowtie2 (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012) for mapping reads to the human genome (hg38) with an average mapping ratio of 70%.
evidence: This describes the tool used for adapter trimming.

claim: Bowtie2 was used for mapping reads to the human genome (hg38) with an average mapping ratio of 70%.
source: We used the AdapterRemoval tool for adapter trimming (Schubert et al., 2016) and Bowtie2 (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012) for mapping reads to the human genome (hg38) with an average mapping ratio of 70%.
evidence: This describes the tool used for read mapping and the mapping efficiency.

claim: The SeqBuster tool was used for miRNA annotation counts and isomiR calling.
source: The SeqBuster tool was used for miRNA annotation counts and isomiR calling (Pantano et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the tool used for miRNA and isomiR identification.

claim: RNAs with fewer than five reads in less than 80% of the samples were filtered out.
source: We filtered out the RNAs with fewer than five reads in less than 80% of the samples.
evidence: This describes the filtering criteria for RNA features.

claim: All isomiRs passed the expression were regarded as bona fide isomiRs.
source: All isomiRs passed the expression were regarded as bona fide isomiRs.
evidence: This describes the criteria for considering isomiRs as valid features.

claim: DESeq2's variance stabilizing normalization function was used to normalize identified RNA counts.
source: We used DESeq2's (Love et al., 2014) variance stabilizing normalization function to normalize identified RNA counts.
evidence: This describes the normalization method used.

claim: The optmatch (v0.9–11) R package selected appropriately matched controls while building models.
source: The optmatch (v0.9–11) R package (Hansen and Klopfer, 2006) selected appropriately matched controls while building models.
evidence: This describes the tool used for matching cases and controls.

claim: LC samples and controls were matched on sex, age at donation, and BDg.
source: Therefore, we matched LC samples and controls on sex, age at donation, and BDg.
evidence: This describes the matching variables used in the study.

claim: BDg is a technical cofounder combining the effect of sample treatment at donation and storage time.
source: BDg is a technical cofounder combining the effect of sample treatment at donation and storage time (Rounge et al., 2018).
evidence: This defines what BDg represents, supported by a citation.

claim: R function kegga from the limma package was used for KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of selected RNA features if they are miRNA, isomiR, or mRNA.
source: We used R function kegga from the limma package for KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of selected RNA features if they are miRNA, isomiR, or mRNA.
evidence: This describes the method used for pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: The miRNA and isomiR targets were extracted from MIRDB (v5.0) predictions (score cutoff >60).
source: The miRNA and isomiR targets were extracted from MIRDB (v5.0) predictions (Wong and Wang, 2015) (score cutoff >60).
evidence: This describes the source of miRNA target predictions.

claim: High dimensionality is often a problem in modeling RNA-seq data.
source: High dimensionality is often a problem in modeling RNA-seq data.
evidence: This is a statement about a common challenge in RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Preliminary analysis showed that ML algorithms with regularization produced successful models.
source: Our preliminary analysis showed that ML algorithms with regularization produced successful models.
evidence: This describes the rationale for selecting specific ML algorithms.

claim: Five ML algorithms were selected to create initial models: lasso, elastic-net, sparse group lasso (SGL), RF, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithms.
source: Therefore, we selected five ML algorithms to create our initial models: lasso, elastic-net, sparse group lasso (SGL), RF, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithms.
evidence: This lists the ML algorithms used in the study.

claim: Fivefold cross-validation (if available) was used to tune hyperparameters for model training.
source: We used fivefold cross-validation (if available) to tune hyperparameters for model training.
evidence: This describes the hyperparameter tuning method.

claim: For the SGL models, RNAs were classified by type.
source: For the SGL models, RNAs were classified by type.
evidence: This describes a specific aspect of the SGL modeling approach.

claim: R implementations of the algorithms were used: caret (v6.0–84) and glmnet (v2.0–18) packages for elastic-net and the lasso, sglfast (v0.10) and msgl (v2.3.9) for the SGL models and xgboost (v1.0.0.2) for XGBoost.
source: R implementations of these algorithms were used: caret (v6.0–84) and glmnet (v2.0–18) packages for elastic-net and the lasso, sglfast (v0.10) and msgl (v2.3.9) for the SGL models and xgboost (v1.0.0.2) for XGBoost.
evidence: This lists the R packages used for implementing the ML algorithms.

claim: Classifications were performed according to histology and time to diagnosis using an automated ML workflow.
source: Classifications were performed according to histology and time to diagnosis (for details see next paragraph) using an automated ML workflow.
evidence: This describes the classification strategy.

claim: In the ML workflow the datasets were split into training (70%) and test (30%).
source: In the ML workflow the datasets were split into training (70%) and test (30%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the data splitting strategy.

claim: The data splitting step was repeated five times using designated seed numbers to select five different training and test datasets which were balanced for case/control numbers and also matched for confounders (i.e. sex, age, and BDg).
source: We repeated this step five times using designated seed numbers to select five different training and test datasets which were balanced for case/control numbers and also matched for confounders (i.e. sex, age, and BDg).
evidence: This describes the repeated data splitting approach to ensure robustness.

claim: Model optimization including hyperparameter tuning was done by a grid search approach followed by fivefold cross-validation using the training sets.
source: Model optimization including hyperparameter tuning was done by a grid search approach followed by fivefold cross-validation using the training sets.
evidence: This describes the model optimization procedure.

claim: The test datasets were only used for testing to overcome overfitting and assess true performance.
source: The test datasets were only used for testing to overcome overfitting and assess true performance.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the test datasets.

claim: The performance of the classifiers were mainly evaluated by area under the ROC curves (AUC)s.
source: The performance of the classifiers were mainly evaluated by area under the ROC curves (AUC)s.
evidence: This describes the primary performance metric.

claim: Accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were also calculated.
source: We also calculated accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.
evidence: This describes additional performance metrics calculated.

claim: Confidence interval calculations were done using metrics of test datasets.
source: Confidence interval calculations were done using metrics of test datasets.
evidence: This describes how confidence intervals were calculated.

claim: Models for all histologies, NSCLC and SCLC that do not take time to diagnose into account are referred to as standard full-time models.
source: We refer to models for all histologies, NSCLC and SCLC that do not take time to diagnose into account as standard full-time models (Figure 1B).
evidence: This defines the terminology used for a specific type of model.

claim: Prediagnostic models were created using a sliding windows approach and a fixed-time approach to find optimal time to diagnose intervals.
source: Prediagnostic models were created using a sliding windows approach and a fixed-time approach to find optimal time to diagnose intervals.
evidence: This describes the approaches used for creating prediagnostic models.

claim: Three different window sizes, 2, 3, and 4 years, were selected which were moved over the 10 years prior to diagnosis time.
source: We first selected three different window sizes, 2, 3, and 4 years, which were moved over the 10 years prior to diagnosis time.
evidence: This describes the sliding window approach parameters.

claim: Models were built based on samples captured by the sliding windows.
source: We then built models based on samples captured by these sliding windows.
evidence: This describes how the sliding window approach was used for modeling.

claim: Fixed-time windows were 0–2, 0–5, and 0–8 years before diagnosis.
source: Fixed-time windows were 0–2, 0–5, and 0–8 years before diagnosis.
evidence: This describes the fixed window approach parameters.

claim: The workflow described was used to train and test both standard and prediagnostic models.
source: We used the workflow described above to train and test both standard and prediagnostic models.
evidence: This describes the consistency of the modeling approach.

claim: Feature selection methods implemented include single-RNA class, lasso selection, and significant selection.
source: We implemented feature selection methods to improve model performances, including single-RNA class, lasso selection, and significant selection.
evidence: This lists the feature selection methods used.

claim: In the single-RNA class method, all RNA types except one were dropped.
source: In the single-RNA class method, we dropped all RNA types except one.
evidence: This describes the single-RNA class feature selection method.

claim: In lasso selection, all non-zero features selected by the lasso classification models were pooled and used to retrain new classification models.
source: In lasso selection, all non-zero features selected by the lasso classification models were pooled. Next, we retrained new classification models which were restricted to use only these features.
evidence: This describes the lasso feature selection method.

claim: In significance selection, an univariate regression analysis was done per feature and significant features (multiple testing adjusted) were used to train classification models.
source: In significance selection, an univariate regression analysis was done per feature and significant features (multiple testing adjusted) were used to train classification models.
evidence: This describes the univariate significance feature selection method.

claim: Models were created for each histology which utilize the most frequent features identified in the standard full-time models.
source: We created models for each histology which utilize the most frequent features identified in the standard full-time models.
evidence: This describes the frequent feature model approach.

claim: To assess overfitting and to get a better estimate of frequent feature model performances, the datasets were split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets.
source: To assess overfitting and to get a better estimate of these model performances, we split the datasets into training (80%) and test (20%) sets.
evidence: This describes the data splitting strategy for frequent feature models.

claim: To the test sets, non-smokers and samples from smokers not previously used in frequency matching were added.
source: To the test sets we also added non-smokers and samples from smokers, but not previously used in frequency matching (number of samples reported in Table 3).
evidence: This describes the composition of the test sets for frequent feature models.

claim: Both unmatchable samples and non-smokers were never used for model building and evaluation which are referred to as leave-out sets.
source: Both unmatchable samples and non-smokers were never used for model building and evaluation which we refer to as leave-out sets.
evidence: This defines the leave-out sets.

claim: The frequent feature model analysis was not repeated five times as in the automated ML workflow.
source: We did not repeat this analysis five times as in the automated ML workflow.
evidence: This describes a difference in the frequent feature model approach.

claim: RRs were calculated using the test sets.
source: RRs were calculated using the test sets.
evidence: This describes how relative risks were calculated.

claim: The optimal threshold was identified in cross-validation.
source: The optimal threshold was identified in cross-validation.
evidence: This describes how the classification threshold was determined.

claim: The R packages cutpointr (v1.0.1) and epitools (v0.5–10.1) were used to calculate RRs.
source: We used the R packages cutpointr (v1.0.1) and epitools (v0.5–10.1) to calculate RRs.
evidence: This lists the R packages used for RR calculations.
